title: How the calendar works
hookLine: solemnities, feasts and memorials, with Sundays at the center

lines: FROM THE BOOK TO THE YEAR.
cards: Open a parish wall calendar and the squares are not all equal. Some days are printed in red. Some have a saint's name in small type.
Some just say Tuesday of the twenty-third week. A few say something stronger, and the whole parish knows it: Christmas, Easter, the Assumption.
The Bible has been read cover to cover; now comes the way the Church hears it, one feast at a time, around a year with its own shape. First, a key.

teach.b: The Church's calendar sorts its days into ranks. At the top is a solemnity, from the Latin sollemnitas, a yearly, festive observance: Christmas, Easter, Pentecost, the Immaculate Conception, Saints Peter and Paul.
A solemnity begins the evening before, the way a Jewish sabbath begins at sunset, and at Mass the Gloria is sung and the Creed is said.
One step down is a feast: an apostle, the Holy Family, the Conversion of Saint Paul. A feast keeps to its own day, with the Gloria and usually without the Creed.
Below that comes a memorial, a saint remembered, some obligatory, some optional. And under them all, the plain weekday, which the books call a feria.

Here's the surprise: Sunday sits at the center. The Second Vatican Council called the Lord's Day the original feast day, kept every week in memory of the resurrection. An ordinary Sunday outranks almost every saint.
The Sundays of Advent, Lent and Easter outrank even most solemnities: when one collides with them, the solemnity moves. An official table, a ladder of thirteen steps, settles every collision.
It sounds like bookkeeping, but the effect is that the year breathes: long green stretches of ordinary weeks, then the purple seasons of waiting, then white and gold for the great days.

teach.h: THIS IS THE DAY WHICH THE LORD HATH MADE.
teach.b: A psalm the Church sings at Easter says it plainly: "This is the day which the Lord hath made: let us be glad and rejoice therein." The calendar says which joy today is. And the year doesn't start in January.

how: Catholics follow the General Roman Calendar, which ranks each day as a solemnity, feast, memorial or weekday; parish calendars, missals and liturgy apps show each day's rank and color.

o: any Sunday Mass with a sung Creed and Gloria
the highest rank of day in the Church's calendar

games.q: a solemnity falls on a Sunday of Advent this year. you're planning the parish Mass. what happens?
o: the solemnity wins and replaces the Sunday.
the Sunday keeps its place and the solemnity moves.

games.why: the Sundays of Advent, Lent and Easter outrank most solemnities. the solemnity is moved to another day, by the official table of precedence.

practice: If you have a missal, a parish calendar or a liturgy app, look up today: a solemnity, a feast, a memorial or a plain weekday, a saint named or not, and what color the priest is wearing. If you can't look it up, just guess.
A plain weekday is not a lesser day, since most of life is lived on them; if you pray, greet today by its name, and if not, just notice that it has one.

wordCard.voice: Solemnity. The highest rank of day in the Catholic calendar, from the Latin sollemnitas, a festive yearly observance. It begins the evening before. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a solemn, yearly festival; the top rank of day in the Roman calendar.

carryVoice: Your line: every day has a rank. Even a plain Tuesday has a name. Day six hundred thirty-two, done.
